utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecution versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to greet everyone in the courtroom. We have to move on rapidly. Time is short. I'll read out two decisions; one concerns the admission into evidence of documents relating to Witness BS. This witness appeared on the 11th of October, 2006. The Chamber, given the requests made by the Prosecution, notes that P 09685, 687, and 688 have already been admitted into evidence. The Chamber admits the following into evidence: P 08405, P 08409, P 08701, P 08900, and P 08901, and P 08903. In addition, the Chamber will admit the following Defence exhibits: 2D 00200. The Chamber also indicates that the following documents must be under seal: P 08405, P 08409, P 08701, P 08900, P 08901, P 08903, and 2D 00200. The Chamber has another decision to render, and I would like both parties to listen very carefully. The Chamber will now render a decision, and it invites the parties to make known their positions with regard to the necessity of adopting new measures in order to complete the proceedings within a reasonable time limit. At a hearing held on the 16th of October, 2006, the Chamber and the parties addressed the issue of the time for the proceedings as decided by the Registry in October -- on the 12th of October, 2006. Following the discussions on the basis of the information provided by the Registry, the Trial Chamber notes that given the pace at which we are working, the Prosecution case will not be completed before the end of March, 2008. The Chamber intends to render a decision in the very near future, a written decision, in which certain measures will be taken in order to complete the Prosecution case within a more reasonable time limit, either before -- before the court recess in the summer of 2007. The Chamber intends to reduce the number of hours allocated to the Prosecution for the presentation of its case. We intend -- the Chamber intends to reduce the number of hours by one-fourth. The Chamber also intends to modify the procedure used when calculating the time used at hearings. The Chamber intends to deduct the time used for raising objections from the time allocated to the party raising the objection in question. The Chamber would similarly like to encourage the parties to have recourse to written motions, especially when these motions concern protective measures and tendering documents into evidence. Prior to adopting such measures, the Chamber would like to hear the parties' oral submissions on -- next Monday, and we should also note that the Prosecution will have 15 minutes at its disposal to make their position known, whereas the Defence will have the same amount of time, roughly speaking. Very briefly, the Prosecution and the Defence have until Monday to reflect on the oral submissions that you will make, and on Monday at 2.15, the Prosecution will take the floor for 15 minutes to inform us of their position, and I will then give the floor to the Defence for 15 minutes. Its's up to you to see how you're going to divide this time amongst yourselves, or perhaps you'll select one representative of the Defence to speak on behalf of all the Defence teams. And in the coming days we'll be rendering a written decision. Our intention is to complete the Prosecution case in July. No comments. You have been provided with all the necessary information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, just one observation, Mr. President. You say that the Chamber intends. Would appear that there's a fait accompli here. I'm wondering whether it's being just -- the Chamber is thinking of it or whether the Chamber has made the decision and we're supposed to respond to this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you are well aware, intentions can be modified. This intention of ours could be modified in the light of the submissions that you will be making. We could render a decision now, but since we are all in favour of adversarial proceedings, we would like to hear the positions of the parties. But we do have an explicit intention and it would be desirable to complete the Prosecution case before court recess in July. And as I have already noted in the decision, that would mean reducing the time allocated to the Prosecution by 100 hours. Mr. Mundis, you'll inform Mr. Scott of everything that has been said. He must be following the proceedings in front of his screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: He is indeed, and I've already received an e-mail from him to that effect. We will certainly be in a position to make the Prosecution's position very well known to the Trial Chamber on Monday commencing at 1415 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to use up time unnecessarily, but perhaps Your Honour would allow me to make one observation very briefly. Recently Mr. Karnavas made a suggestion that perhaps the time had come to hold a Status Conference or a 65 ter Conference to consider a number of matters arising about the conduct of the trial. Obviously the decision that Your Honours are thinking of taking has considerable ramifications, both for the Prosecution and the Defence. There issues of fairness will arise to both sides. And in addition, the Trial Chamber has already instructed us to make submissions about modifications of the Trial Chamber's decision on evidence of the 13th of July. And, Your Honour, if I may respectfully make the submission that perhaps the time has come to -- to take up Mr. Karnavas's suggestion and devote perhaps a little more time than 15 minutes per side, and perhaps that could be done at a time when it would not interrupt the normal working of the trial. If the Court has some time where we could even meet perhaps in a meetingroom as opposed to the courtroom if that would be helpful. But, Your Honour, the issues here are very serious, and we would ask for a more leisurely exchange of views than the Trial Chamber has indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Last time the Chamber asked Mr. Karnavas to provide the Legal Officer with a list of the issues that he wanted to address. So far we haven't received such a list, I'm quite persuaded that Mr. Karnavas is working on it and it will be provided to us. But a meeting might be useful for the implementation of the decision that will be rendered. We really have to bring the witness into the courtroom now. We will now ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Mundis has 40 or 45 minutes left at his disposal, and the Defence teams have one hour for Mr. Petkovic, an hour for Mr. Praljak, and 35 minutes for the other Defence teams, unless you agree on dividing the time amongst yourselves in a different manner. But the hearing will be adjourned tomorrow at 7.00 p.m; that is absolutely necessary. Yes, Mr. Mundis. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we call the witness into the courtroom -- or before he comes into the courtroom I'd like to mention an exhibit that I should tender with relation to the witness Kurbegovic. It concerns the list of those wounded or killed among the HVO members. It was signed by a certain Kraljevic. It's an HVO brigade document, the Ante Starcevic Brigade document. You asked us whether we'd be tendering this document into evidence; we said we would. It's in the e-court system now and the number is 3D 00476 and I would like tender this document into evidence, in particular because this is a document that will probably be used with this witness too. Since I have interrupted the Bench, I'd also like to mention that we have in e-court 3D 00463 document. This is a document you asked about when Mr. Praljak tendered the map number IC 42 it was used for Witness Hauenstein. On that occasion you asked us to provide you with the markings for the legend for the map, the legend is according to NATO standards, but when we were investigating matters we found another document 3D 00465 is the number of that we have it in the e-court system. In case the Bench would have reasons to go into this subject matter, then this other document might be of assistance it hasn't been translated because it's quite voluminous and it wasn't possible to do that. But document 463 is the one that you asked about, so perhaps it could be linked to document IC 42 and I think we have now done what we wanted to do. Mr. Praljak will be using a map today, and again the same symbols will be used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Brigadier Agic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I see that you still have the bundle of documents in front of you, and to avoid wasting any further time I would ask if you could please turn to document 1172. Sir, when was the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you were discussing with us the types of weapons that were used in Gornji Vakuf. Can you comment on this document, 1172, in light of what you told us about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this concerns the nitroglycerine rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question that I would like to put to you. The rifles that used nitroglycerine or nitroglycerine bullets, are they sanctioned by the International Convention on Arms, are they authorised -- is their use authorised by this convention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I wouldn't know how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier Agic, this document bears the name of General Praljak at the bottom. Were you familiar or aware of any other names that General Praljak went by?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would call him Brada.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you perhaps tell us why he was called Brada.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a while when he used the communications system he had this secret name, Brada, and that's why we took this to be General Praljak's nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What does the name Brada mean in your language?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't mean anything in particular. It means the man has a beard; "Brada" is "beard."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please turn to exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying something that's quite interesting, so I can't pass over what you've just said. You said it's because of the communications system that you found out that when General Praljak had contact with other officers he used this secret name "Brada" or beard. So can I assume that the ABiH had the technical means to intercept the communications, the radio or telephone communications or other forms of communications used by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My unit didn't have those means, but other armija units did. If you're on the same frequency when carrying out investigations, yes, it's possible to intercept such communications; it really isn't a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, could you please now turn to document 1183. And again, Brigadier Agic, as a preliminary matter when was the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in light of your testimony yesterday, can you comment on this document, particularly the reference to an attack on Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Makljen.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here they're referring to the evacuation of the wounded from Bugojno. You should be aware of the fact that at the beginning of the war a joint war hospital was established in Bugojno, and it was used to treat the wounded of the armija of Bosnia and Herzegovina and members of the HVO. As far as combat in the direction of Makljen is concerned, well, that was during a certain period, the 18th of January. The HVO was making efforts to gain control of the town. And the threat referred to here, well, that's probably a message for Bugojno, because the telegram went to the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please turn to the document marked 1213. Sir, when was the first time you saw this document, 1213?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not sure -- because I can see the document you're looking at, I'm not sure, sir, if we're on the same document. I'm now going to ask you to look at 1213.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just to be clear for the record, when was the first time you saw this document, 1213?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, again yesterday you were talking about some of the villages around Gornji Vakuf. Can you comment on this document, in light of what you told us about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this. I was familiar with this at the time of the conflict. It's true that Dusa was set on fire. I think 12 civilians were killed. The armija didn't have any soldiers in this area. We had soldiers in the village of Uzricje. We managed to withdraw some of them in an organised manner in the course of an intensive attacked launched by the HVO. We managed to withdraw some of the men in the direction of Uzricje; Kuk, the repeater; and Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier Agic, can you now turn to 1226, please. When was the first time you saw this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again in light of your testimony yesterday and earlier today, can you comment on this document relating to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document from the 3rd Corps command was drafted on the basis of an operative report that the 317th Brigade had forwarded, forwarded such reports to the Cikotic Brigade since they were in UNPROFOR and they were constantly trying to put an end to the conflict in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you've been discussing the conflict in Gornji Vakuf, and yesterday you mentioned a number of efforts concerning cease-fire discussions. Can you tell us, sir, if there came a time when any cease-fires came into effect in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A cease-fire came into effect on -- on the 21st, but on the 22nd it wasn't respected. The UNPROFOR and a delegation was visited by General Morillon. He tried to explain to the delegation within UNPROFOR that the political delegations of the Croatian and Bosniak people were preparing to have a meeting in Geneva, and as a result it would be good to maintain the status quo in Gornji Vakuf while the high-level political state bodies were trying to solve the issue of provinces. General Praljak [as interpreted] responded by saying that he wouldn't withdraw with his troops. He said that he had the authority to regroup and that it wasn't necessary to fill in the trenches because he had taken them. And then General Morillon warned Colonel Siljeg and told him that he had to abide by the order issued by General Petkovic. I don't know what kind of order was in question, but he told him that he had to respect General Petkovic's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since we know what the witness has already said about this document and since we're familiar with his statement, I assume that he mistakenly said General Praljak. I think he's referring to Siljeg. Perhaps my learned friend could check this. It's at the beginning of the paragraph, line 20 on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it Colonel Siljeg who answered General Morillon, or was it General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. General Praljak wasn't present there; it was Colonel Siljeg who answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I made a mistake. I apologise to General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier Agic, this cease-fire that came into effect on the 21st of January, 1993, what preparatory steps were taken in order to reach that agreement?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the agreements of the 21st following the visit of General Morillon for these decisions to be implemented on the ground, certain commissions were formed, a commission for supervising the cease-fire and commissions that would supervise the digging -- the filling in of the trenches. And a part of the personnel from the HVO in Bugojno and from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, also from Bugojno, were deployed on different sides, that is, army representatives went to HVO units and representatives of the HVO came to army units in Gornji Vakuf. However, on the ground then couldn't carry out everything, because I know for certain that certain officers who were in Pidris, in the evening UNPROFOR pulled them back because it was impossible for them to work and they were in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, sir. My question perhaps wasn't as clear as it should have been. I'm interested in knowing the developments in the few days before the agreement came into effect; in other words, what steps, if any, were the parties taking that resulted in the 21 January 1993 cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such efforts were made throughout January, ever since the conflict started, to put an end to it; but on the 20th it was actually agreed that conditions should be ensured for a cease-fire. Discussions were held at the UNPROFOR base headquarters, and the chairperson on behalf of the European Union was Ambassador Bousseau and Colonel Stewart represented UNPROFOR. Present on behalf of the army was Selmo Cikotic, and on behalf of the HVO Colonel Siljeg and two new officers who I did not know at the time. And the discussion was about the first steps that should be taken. Siljeg's response to Ambassador Bousseau was, "If you had come 24 hours later, there would have been no need to discuss this cease-fire." Throughout the time Colonel Siljeg behaved as if he had power and support behind him and he could do whatever he wanted and achieve his goal, and that is to control Gornji Vakuf. However, an agreement was reached for the cease-fire to come into force on the 21st, I think at 1200 hours. And this cease-fire signed on the 21st, in spite of all efforts that had been made to stop the fighting, did not hold.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you please turn to document 1203. When was first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see this one, but with respect to this report, after this report we received an order ordering what was suggested here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention, sir, to the paragraph that begins in your language "prijedlog o prekidu." Do you see that, the proposal on cease-fire in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This related to the preparation of a draft agreement before Ambassador Bousseau arrived. This was done because an UNPROFOR member presided; if it wasn't Colonel Stewart, then it would be Major Colm Doyle in Gornji Vakuf who would preside over the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This document from General Hadzihasanovic indicates the proposal on cease-fire in Gornji Vakuf should be accepted. And my question to you, sir, is, if you know: Who put forward this proposal?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a proposal made at a commission meeting, and probably a part of this report by General Hadzihasanovic for the Supreme Command Staff was based on a report sent to him on a daily basis by a member of the corps who was at UNPROFOR, and that is Selmo Cikotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, can you now turn to document 1229, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry for this technical failure. I would only like to clarify one issue here. On page 2 of document 1203, the very first line in the English version the sentence reads that: "To return all soldiers from Livno, Duvno, Posusje, Tomislavgrad, and Split without exceptions." Probably it is due to my failure in -- in the -- to knowing the places over there, but I found Split -- is it Split in the Croatian side that is Split, the sea, or there is another smaller province, one of township Split, and in that -- in that place which is around, I believe, Gornji Vakuf, et cetera? That is my question, only geographical issue. It is what I would like to ask the witness Brigadier Agic about it. Of course this -- this order was issued by Enver Hadzihasanovic, so I believe it is Split which is not related to the Split of Croatia. But anyway, if you could confirm this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Split in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is to Mr. Mundis. In document 1229, you were going to ask the witness about an agreement signed by Siljeg, Cikotic, Bousseau, Stewart, and I note that the English document has no signature and the document in B/C/S has no signature. Apparently the B/C/S document is a translation. What is the -- where is the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd have to make some inquiries on that, Your Honour, but perhaps the witness might be able to assist us with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, do you have 1229 before you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you present at any meetings when this document was discussed and/or drafted?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it written, and this is how it was compiled. It was a cease-fire that was signed, and that should have come into effect on the 21st of January at 1200 hours. It says here the 22nd, but I think it's a mistake. I think it was meant to come into force on the 21st, but I said that General Morillon came on the 23rd, and the cease-fire was not achieved on the basis of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, if you -- could you take a look, please, at paragraph A of this document.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. It says that it should start at 1700. As far as I know, it should have started at 1200 hours, because I received an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you mentioned that this cease-fire was signed. Did you actually see a signed version of this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. It was no secret. All those present were very glad to have it. At least that was my opinion. Maybe there were certain individuals who were an exception. It was signed, and at the time it was a relief for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you document that you saw, was it in English or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw a version in the language that I understood, and that is the B/C/S language. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have the signed document, and I can provide it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us, did this cease-fire take effect for any period of time at all?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Please take a look at document 1291. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this one, but I saw another document regulating the admission of these two new persons, Esad Ramic and Emin Bijedic, members of the 1st Corps. My assignment was to ensure through UNPROFOR their arrival in Voljevac for them to be brought to UNPROFOR headquarters in Gornji Vakuf, and this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was -- first of all, who were Esad Ramic and Mr. Bijedic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esad Ramic was a commander of Municipal Staff in Konjic, and Emin Bijedic was a member of the command of the 4th Corps. And I think there were sent to Gornji Vakuf for the negotiations to benefit from earlier experiences, and I think General Pasalic's proposal was accepted, that he sent these two officers in the hope that some progress would be made in the negotiations, because General Pasalic and General Petkovic had resolved certain similar matters in this way in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, how long were these two individuals, Mr. Ramic and Mr. Bijedic, in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I won't be wrong if I say that they stayed until about the 20th or 24th of February, 1993, and they were part of a team who prepared the cease-fire, which you will see eventually was signed by General Petkovic and General Arif Pasalic on behalf of the armija and General Petkovic on behalf of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This cease-fire -- this cease-fire that you're referring to that was signed by Generals Petkovic and Pasalic, when was that document signed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed -- I didn't understand the interpreter. I think it was signed on the 14th or the 15th of February at UNPROFOR headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me return, sir, to this document 1291 and what's reported in this document. My question for you, sir, is: During the time period that these two gentlemen, Mr. Ramic and Mr. Bijedic, were in Gornji Vakuf, did you at any point in time brief them on the situation in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the authority to brief them, but they were briefed by the team of the armija. I think Mr. Cikotic informed them about the stage of the negotiations and the general situation in the territory of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me draw your attention to a couple of points that are made in this document. If you could look at the bottom of the first page you'll see towards the very bottom references to a number of villages in Gornji Vakuf municipality. Can you take a look at that part of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Pidris, Mackovac, Baban?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you comment on that part of this document, what's reflected in this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the facts are correct and these are the locations where the strongest HVO units were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you look a little bit farther down you'll see references to other villages including Zdrimci, Dusa, and Uzricje. Do you see that part of the document? It was actually I believe on the bottom of the first page, sir.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two lines are missing in my copy, but in those days, the 24th of January, Zdrimci and Dusa and Uzricje were captured by the HVO, the houses torched, the population taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, could you please take a look at document 1333. When was the first time, Brigadier Agic, that you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document when I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment, please, on the part of this report under paragraph number 1.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the figure of 110 persons from Hrasnica is not correct. I think it was 120 or 121 persons. In Zdrimci, I think the number is smaller. According to my information, it was between 13 and 15 persons. As for Uzricje and Dusa, I'm not sure, but I believe it wasn't 40 [as interpreted] persons that were killed in Dusa. I think between 8 and 12, so I'm not sure. But I'm sure about Hrasnica, that the number was 121, because during the exchange in March that was how many people we exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear here, sir, this document is referring to the capture and detention of Muslim civilians, but the transcript just indicated that you -- at least in English that you were referring to 40 persons that were killed in Dusa. Were 40 persons killed in Dusa, or were 40 persons detained -- captured and detained in Dusa?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twelve persons were killed in Dusa according to the army's records. As for the detained persons, it couldn't be 40 because there weren't 40 people there. I have to say this with some reservation for the following reasons: In these settlements there were refugees who were -- I won't say out of control - but on their own initiative or through their relations came there after the conflicts in Jajce and Donji Vakuf when the Serbian Montenegrin aggressor captured those towns, and then those persons came to Gornji Vakuf through their own personal connections. So I can't be very specific when talking about these numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please, sir, look at the information contained right after the reference to Dusa where there's reference to 222 persons. Could you comment on that part of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were more persons detained in the furniture factory and the secondary school in Prozor, counting the people who at the beginning of the conflict who were stopped on the road and detained, people who were returning from visits to the family and other people who happened to be on the road and were detained for no reason. So that I think the number was more than 220. But what I can say with certainty is that in Hrasnica there were 121 persons who were detained and taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Please take a look, sir, at document 1433. And again, when was the first time you saw this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it when I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the information set forth in this combat report, can you please comment particularly with respect to the information concerning Uzricje, Zdrimci, Dusa, and Krupa?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was regular practice. When a territory was captured, fires would burn all night, and I think that HVO soldiers by using incendiary bullets and -- wanted to torch as many buildings as possible, and thus cause fear and have a negative impact on members of the armija to help them decide to withdraw from Gornji Vakuf as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please take a look, sir, at document 1567. When was the first time you saw this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you look, please, at the bottom of the document under the last bullet point according to the report. Do you see that portion of the document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment, sir, on that aspect of this document in light of the situation in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after the cease-fire, and then commissions were persistent. There were some minor problems because people returned to their burned homes because they had no where else to go, and there were some minor excesses, but by joint efforts the situation was placed under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before I show you the last document, let me ask you this: You testified yesterday about the presence of HVO military police units in Gornji Vakuf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did there ever come a time, sir, when you learned the identity of those military police officers from the HVO who were present in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to identity we didn't know, but we knew that these were units of the military police of the HVO who had come from parts of Herzegovina, from western and eastern -- no, not eastern, Tomislavgrad and Livno, but we didn't know their identity. We knew that a part of the personnel came also from the region of Gornji Vakuf, because the Ante Starcevic Brigade had its own military police, and we knew those police officers whom we had cooperated with. These were all former members of the TO who before the war had attended exercises jointly. So in Vakuf people knew who were strangers and who were locals who came from some any other area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is something that it is hard to conceal in Bosnia-Herzegovina; people know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, I would like to show you one final document which is numbered 1298. Now, sir, when was the first time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The document is rather lengthy. I would ask you, sir, if you could please turn to the page in your language bearing the numbers that end in 22 at the top. This is page 2 of the English version of the document. Sir, do you recognise the names of any of the individuals listed on this page of this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person under number 6, Ivan Peric, could be from Gornji Vakuf; also, the person under number 14, Kristo; and also the person under 16, Ivica Jurcevic. The other names are not inhabitants of Gornji Vakuf. You can't find these surnames in the census of the population of Gornji Vakuf. I assume that the unit was manned on an ex-territorial principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could finally then turn to the page of this document in your language bearing number 33 at the top. This is page 12 in the English version. Brigadier Agic, do you recognise any of the names of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Number 1, the commander of the military police in Gornji Vakuf, Miro Bandic, from the village of Podgradje; a pre-war policeman from Bugojno. All the other names are people from Gornji Vakuf, from the area of Gornji Vakuf, and I know many of these who are more or less my age. There are a few individuals such as the Branislav Subasic under number 24; he wasn't in Gornji Vakuf. There were no Subasics in Gornji Vakuf. Number 38, Barisic, the Barisics aren't from Gornji Vakuf. The individual under number 39, Herceg, wasn't from there. All the other family names are family names from Gornji Vakuf, from the municipality of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Brigadier Agic, I'd like to thank you for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further direct examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you could perhaps inform us of the numbers of the exhibits that you'll be tendering and then we will have the break after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will tender documents -- and I'll just read either the last three or four digits to avoid confusion: 643, 712, 1087, 1107, 1132, 1126, 1131, 1174, 1146, 1135, 1139, 1172, 1183, 1213, 1226, 1203, 1229, 1291, 1333, 1433, 1567, 1298. And if the Trial Chamber would just indulge me for one moment, Your Honour. We have one issue arising from a document that was shown to the witness Andrew Williams, which was again shown to the witness but which one of my colleagues unintentionally neglected to tender, that was P 1311 [Realtime transcript read in error "311"], which was again was shown to the witness Williams a few days ago. And also just prior to the break, I'd like to inform the Trial Chamber and all the parties that prior to this current session we distributed the calendar of scheduled witnesses that will take us through to the winter recess on the 14th December. And I've provided that to the Chamber's Legal Officers as well and I wanted to inform the Chamber as well, so we have the court schedule through the 14th of December. Thank you. My colleague informs me that the document for Williams wasn't reflected it should be 1311. 1311 was the document that we showed to the witness Williams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it in the e-court system? Yes or no? This document is a document you want to show the witness so that he can recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just wanted to, before a decision was taken on the Williams exhibits, inform the Chamber that we had shown that to Mr. Williams but unintentionally didn't tender that document formally, so we would ask that that be admitted into evidence. We have no more documents for this witness; we have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We object to tendering P 0 -- P 10 -- P 1298 for a number of reasons because it's a very voluminous document and the two pages of this document was shown to the witness, and the request is being made for the entire document to be admitted. If you have a look at the B/C/S version, you can see that this document consists of a number of documents in fact, so it's very difficult to determine the period that the document relates to, and in particular because two of the pages that were shown to the witness don't bear any dates so the time-period that the list relates to. The Intervention Platoon of the military police in Gornji Vakuf is the title, but we know which time-period is concerned, there is no stamp, no signature. And on the page that refers to the composition of the military police in Gornji Vakuf it's also impossible to find a date. So we don't know how the witness could identify it and in relation to which period it will be possible for him to do so. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We take note of that. It's 20 past 3.00. We will have our 20-minute break, and then the Defence can commence with its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the first Defence team now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have no cross-examination for the gentleman, though this decision not to cross-examine should not be interpreted, as was suggested by Mr. Mundis that yesterday I was conducting my cross-examination during his direct through my objections. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas, for that information. And now for the next Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good day. My name is Vesna Alaburic, I'm a lawyer from Zagreb, and I represent General Milivoj Petkovic in these proceedings. I have some questions I'd like to put to you, and I'm sure that you will help us understand the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If I have understood you correctly, yesterday you were saying that a Croat, Mr. Mladen Kovacevic, was elected as the head of the TO in Gornji Vakuf, and you directly link this to the multi-party elections that had been held and that recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state. There are just a few details that I would like to clarify because I don't believe it's been clearly noted in the transcript. The first elections were in November 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At a national level -- I'm waiting for the transcript. It was both at a state level and at a local level; is that correct? These elections were held at the same time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There's a multi-party agreement in the area of Gornji Vakuf, and as a result the head of the Territorial Defence was supposed to be an HDZ member. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That means that at the end of 1990, Mr. Mladen Kovacevic was appointed as the, or rather, chief of the Gornji Vakuf TO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st or 2nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And who held that position in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So according to this multi-party agreement, how is it that the main position in the TO went to an HDZ member? Were you an HDZ member?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the multi-party agreement wasn't respected?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The multi-party agreement was respected, but I remained in that position until the end of March 1992. I was relieved of my duties pursuant to a decision of the Municipal Assembly on that day, and the president of the Executive Committee, Mr. Miro Batinic, had the authority to take a decision and allowed me to continue performing my duties for a certain period of time. There are two reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is not really important for us. At the moment the reasons aren't that important. I just want to know why that happened. I'd also like to clarify something for the Judges with regard to -- to the establishment of the Territorial Defence of the independent state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We mentioned that subject yesterday, and I'd like to discuss this in relation to certain documents now. Please have a look in my bundle of documents at document number 4D 00414.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have that document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 4D 00414. This is a decree on disbanding the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence and on establishing a staff of Territorial Defence in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the document that I mentioned yesterday that was adopted on the 8th of April, 1992, by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you familiar with this decree?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this is in fact the decree that was issued, that was implemented, that was adopted?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now have a look at 4D 00411. This is a decision from the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on linking up all the armed forces in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have it on the screen in the e-court system. According to that decision, all armed units and individuals were requested to report to Territorial Defence Staffs in order to be placed under a single command. That's what's stated under item 1. In item 4, the date is mentioned by which this task should be carried out. The date is the 15th of April, 1992. Were you familiar with this decision, with the contents of this decision?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and on the 15th of April -- well, that's when -- that's the official date on which the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina were established. That's correct. We'll see that's this is also confirmed by law.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When this decision was taken on the 9th of April, which armed forces were in existence? Which of the armed forces that were to report to the Territorial Defence staffs, since one day earlier the former Territorial Defence had been disbanded? In other words, could you confirm that on that day the following armed forces exist: The Green Berets. Were the Green Berets present as an armed force in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was there a force called the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And these armed forces, the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, did they respond to this decision and did they become part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Patriotic League in Gornji Vakuf did respond, and they placed themselves under the command of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now have a look at 4D 00407. This is a decree, decree -- 409. I apologise. This is a decree with the force of law on armed forces on the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was adopted on the 20th of May, 1992, and in Article 36 it says that on the 15th of April, or rather, the 15th of April shall be taken to be the day on which the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, just as you have said.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's sufficient to clarify certain matters, to show that in fact the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in a certain sense was composed of the armed forces of the Patriotic League, of the Green Berets, and other armed forces. These are units that responded to the request to place themselves under Territorial Defence staffs by the 15th of April. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please have a look at 4D 00404. This is an order from the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was adopted at a meeting held on the 23rd of June, 1992. And in this order it decided to change the name Territorial Defence into the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you familiar -- were you familiar with the contents of this order?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2 says: "The Territorial Defence shall be changed into the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Item 1 says: "The name Territorial Defence shall be changed into Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be established."

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I know what the difference between armed forces and an army is, but on this occasion I don't think it's of much importance for me. If the Judges would like to discuss the matter, I have all the rules on the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina at hand. I would now like to discuss a document that relates to my client, General Milivoj Petkovic. It's a document that you mentioned yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. One of the documents we have seen states that all the forces should be recorded. I think it's Article 4. It says that all those who fail to be recorded would be considered as paramilitary units and may be susceptible to punishment, et cetera. As far as you know, were there any forces that didn't become part of the Territorial Defence at the time that they were obliged to comply with this request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know about other areas, but that was not the case in Gornji Vakuf; there were no such forces in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So at least the situation is clear as far as Gornji Vakuf is concerned. It's clear in light of what you have said. Perhaps the Defence has other information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I think that we could discuss the subject of the HVO and the relationship with the Territorial Defence. I'll deal with that perhaps if I have time to address those issues too. Please have a look at Prosecution Exhibit - you have it in the bundle of Prosecution documents - P 01087; it's an order from Milivoj Petkovic dated the 9th of January, 1993. The order concerns raising the level of combat readiness because of the negotiations to be held in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1087, or rather, are you referring to this brief order, this short order?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I understood your testimony correctly, you commented on this order and said that it was a document that showed that the alleged attack by the HVO on Gornji Vakuf had been planned. I'd like to draw your attention to a number of facts. Can you tell us who this order was forwarded to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that there are three operative zones mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it was forwarded to all three operative zones and not just to the operative zone in Gornji Vakuf. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now have a look at the bundle of documents that I have provided you with. Have a look at 4D 00416 we don't have this document in the e-court system; if necessary we could place the document on the ELMO. The Judges and the Prosecution have copies. This is an order in Zeljko Siljeg dated the 9th of January, 1993. He refers to General Petkovic's order that we have discussed and says because of the upcoming negotiations in Geneva he orders that the level of combat readiness be raised, and this is because the Chetniks have reinforced their units in certain sectors. That's what it says in that order. Do you have any information according to which the HVO and perhaps your armija were raising the level of combat readiness because of the negotiations in Geneva and also in relation to the activities of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the line towards Kupres that we held - and the HVO was to the left of us - in that area there were no signs that the Army of Republika Srpska was raising the level of combat readiness and preparing for combat. But General Petkovic in his order to raise the level of combat readiness -- well, in the preamble he mentions that this should be done because of the negotiations that are upcoming in Geneva and not because of the aggression of the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I think things will be clearer when we have a look at documents from your armija, document 4D 00394; we also have it in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. 4D 00394. This is a warning from the commander of the 4th Corps, Arif Pasalic, and it also has to do with the peace conference in Geneva. Have a look at the fourth line from the bottom; it has to do with the document from the chief of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 5th of January. And in this warning Arif Pasalic is also warning of the possibility of the Serbian army engaging in military action. The entire document is important, but I'd like to draw your attention to the third paragraph. "Given the experience to date with the aggressor, one should expect that the aggressor up until the continuation of the negotiations will try to be militarily successful and will intensify combat in the battlefields that we are already familiar with." In brackets we have certain names. "As a result, it is essential to take certain measures to raise the level of combat readiness and to ensure that we are not taken by surprise. Wherever possible, it's necessary to launch attacks because any military success is a significant contribution to military and political victory over the aggressor." Tell me, were there similar thoughts in your operative zone?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a warning or an order can -- related to a warning from the Main Staff is not something that I receive. Here they mention Gradacac, Brcko, Tesanj, and particularly Sarajevo and East Bosnia. They never mention battlefields in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it is -- it does concern the commander of the 4th Corps. Nevertheless, you quite frequently mentioned that General Petkovic and Pasalic tried to reach agreements, solve problems in a peaceful way. Did they also agree on issuing such orders and warnings with regard to raising the level of combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at a Prosecution exhibit in the Prosecution set of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, this document of the 6th of January, which refers to another document, top secret, of the information service, document VKOSRBH, number 443 of the 5th of January, 1993. Have you studied this document? Have you had this document? Because it says here that this warning was taken or issued on the basis of this document. In view of the fact that the witness says that this had to do with the Serbs, but in the area of Gradacac, Brcko, Tesanj, but not Gornji Vakuf. So it should be interesting to see whether the document which has inspired General Pasalic, does this document have a general bearing on the situation or an area that was not -- that would not include Gornji Vakuf? Well, I'm just telling you about it. Perhaps you will have time to study this document yourself, because I don't have it. But I have just discovered that it exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my introduction to my question I said that the Commander Pasalic issued this warning precisely on the basis of this document. Unfortunately, I do not have that document at my disposal. It is an order by Mr. Sefer Halilovic, and I hope that in due time we will obtain that document and we will be able to tender it to Your Honours. So we know that it refers to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it would be logical to assume that this order applies to the whole territory under the control of Mr. Halilovic. I am told, quite rightly, that this document was addressed to all units, so therefore it's not a question of just locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. But a little question on my part: The 317th Brigade, when it was formed did you depend on the 4th Corps or the 3rd Corps of General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The armed forces in Gornji Vakuf were constantly subordinated to the 3rd Corps throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was it normal then for you to receive documents of the 4th Corps which was not in your chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And were -- were you familiar with the activities of Mr. Arif Pasalic, who was commander of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just a moment, please. General Petkovic perhaps will clarify things for us. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this order Arif Pasalic is listing the localities of the most probable attacks by the Serbs; they're not in the zone of the 4th Corps. He's just drawing attention to his forces that there may be attacks here but also in their zone. Secondly, Sefer Halilovic sent an order to the entire army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; therefore, the commander of the 3rd Corps must have issued a similar order. It's another matter that we can't gain insight into the documents of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sefer Halilovic at that time felt that Brcko, Tesanj, and those places were in the greatest danger, but he doesn't exclude the possibility of such attacks all over the front, Kupres, Bugojno, Jajce, in Eastern Herzegovina, et cetera. Therefore, all corps commands were addressed by this order. He refers to the general order of Sefer Halilovic dated the 5th of January. That is my explanation, because the places Pasalic mentions are not in the area of his corps. But it is the assessment of the political and military leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina that during the talks the Serbs may attempt to gain control of these parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but attacks on other parts are not excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petkovic, for your contribution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We can now look at this new document, Prosecution Exhibit that we discussed yesterday; the number is P 01135. It is an order by General Milivoj Petkovic, who was in those days still a brigadier, dated the 15th of January, 1993. And yesterday we spoke about the preamble of this order referring to the aggression of Muslim forces throughout the territory of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said 1135?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1135. Mention is made of dozens of dead and a large number of wounded, the burning of Croatian houses, and the expulsion of Croats as a reason for issuing this order. I see you have it in front of you. From the contents of this order as we mentioned yesterday and from the indication on page 2 as to who are the addressees, one can conclude that this is an order applying to the entire territory of Herceg-Bosna; is that right? It was addressed to all operative zones.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In view of your interpretation yesterday of this preamble, were you aware that in other municipalities in the territory of Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the situation in Prozor, Novi Travnik, and Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What other municipalities of Herceg-Bosna? You were not aware of the situation there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have any information about the number of killed and wounded fighters of the HVO when this order was issued in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you have or do you have now the figures regarding the number of Croatian houses burnt?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have facts about the expulsion of Croats in those days?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to conclude, then, that you have no information about the facts on the basis of which this order was issued?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that a single Croat house in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf was torched up to this date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at documents on the basis of which this order was issued, but point of clarification first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm wondering -- you appear to have said that you are familiar with the situation in Gornji Vakuf but you didn't know what was happening elsewhere. You belonged to the 3rd Corps in January, and the leader was General Hadzihasanovic. And General Hadzihasanovic, did he rally his brigade commanders to review the situation in the whole zone covered by the 3rd Corps, and then with your colleagues, commanders of other brigades, you would discuss and present your -- the local situation? Unless you never attended a command meeting at the level of the 3rd Corps in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I told Defence counsel that I was familiar with the situation in Prozor, Novi Travnik, and Bugojno; these are neighbouring municipalities. After the new year, that is after the 1st of January, 1993, until this period, I did not go for briefings to the 3rd Corps because in those days it was difficult to get there for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That is why I won't show you documents relating to other municipalities in Herceg-Bosna, but let us look at the documents that reached the Supreme Staff of the HVO. Tell me, when commander Sefer Halilovic, for instance, writes a report or an order or something relevant to a particular area, does he do so on the basis of reports that he receives from his subordinates in the area?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the reports going to the higher command, are they important for the decisions taken by the commander?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but other data are used too. High levels have other possibilities and ways of collecting information and passing decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Certainly they will use information from all possible sources. Let us look first at the report in my set of documents, 4D 00352, and this is a report of the information service in the operative zone of North-western Herzegovina. And for Gornji Vakuf, it says briefly that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- which is referred to as an ally, and please note this - that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is deploying members of their troops in several places in the municipality, in Voljevac, 50 to 61 persons; in Odvode, one unit; and in Voljica, a unit of 200 men in the elementary school. Tell me, are these figures about BH units in Jajce correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not. This unit in this period of time, it numbered between 300 and 400 men, and Rahman was not a person of any authority. The commander of the 305th Brigade was Mr. Halil Dedic, who was a pre-war active-duty officer. And the 305th Brigade started to be formed on the basis of an order, and on the 5th of January it was totally disarmed. They had no weapons whatsoever. And in that area when they were given permission to deploy, they discussed with Gornji Vakuf. Approval was given by Zrinko Tokic as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I am not trying to say anything. Just tell me. In the territory of Gornji Vakuf there were members of the BH army from Jajce, were there not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look now at another document, 4D 00354; it is an order by the Chief of Staff, Brigadier Petkovic, to Zrinko Tokic, asking him to describe relations between the HVO and its allies, that is the BH army, to report about the arrival of fresh forces of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and if there are any blockades of the passage towards Travnik. Tell me, were you aware of attempts by the Main Staff to collect complete information about the situation in the territory of Gornji Vakuf? Did you perhaps talk to Mr. Zrinko Tokic about this?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 11th of January, so I assume that -- this was something that General Petkovic was interested in, that is the situation in the municipality. However, I think this first sentence describe relations between you and the allies does not apply to the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because in the second paragraph it says, "Inform us whether there have been fresh forces of the armija," and I think this applies to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But tell me, who are the allies then?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that had arrived, that is HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How can HVO units be allies of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If that is your interpretation of an alliance. Will you look at the next document, 355. It is a report about the situation in Gornji Vakuf to the Main Staff in connection with the issue we discussed a moment ago. I suggest you read it, and in the meantime I will highlight four points, though there are others. They are reporting to the Main Staff that there is concentration of forces and especially of the BH army, who are deploying in their settlements, Voljevac, Grnica, Vojska, Uzricje, and in the city itself. Then it goes on to say that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 9th of January, received an order from superior commands, that is from the 3rd Corps headquarters --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know which document you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find the text you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I see it on the screen. This is the wrong document. Please look at the screen. Maybe it hasn't been marked properly. I will read it. I started by saying: "On the 9th of January, they received an order from the superior command, that is the 3rd Corps command, that no motor vehicles with troops with move through the territory of Gornji Vakuf without the approval of the 3rd Corps command." Then a little lower down, the third row from the bottom that we see on the screen --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could it be moved for me to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: "Today on the 11th of January in Marsal Tito Street in front of the old hotel, which is in their zone, they have fortified with logs and they have housed the Staff Command in a building there." And in the sixth or seventh row it says: "In addition BH army units in Gornji Vakuf are on full alert, and in the evening they are taking control of certain features." Can you tell us, please, with regard to the contents of this report, if you could very briefly, tell us just what is correct and incorrect.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the commander of the 317th Brigade is well placed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So nothing else is correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true that they came from Travnik and that they were at check-points, it is not true that there was so much movement, and it is not true that units from Jajce were deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that it is not true that there was so much movement. Then tell us: How great was the movement?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on this day, or maybe a day earlier, there was a change of shifts at Radusa. And because of problems in communications, they had to take a roundabout route, and what is claimed here -- could I have it enlarged, please. This reference to the order banning passage is partially true. The corps command did issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. As time is running out, let us move on to the next document, number 4D 0044. This is again an -- a report. As the number is just 44, it should be at the beginning of your bundle.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No. No. It's an intelligence report.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my bundle it's an order to change the name of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher assist for us to place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you can read it from the screen we can give you a hard copy as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it's an intelligence report of the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade dated the 12th of January, and it says: "The Muslim forces have blocked the communication between Ugljen and Gornji Vakuf in places called Drazev and Duratbegovic Dolac. Units from Granica have captured five soldiers from the Ludvig Pavlovic unit in Jajce where fierce battles are taking place. Units of the BH army from Voljica, Osidruk [phoen], using 82-millimetre mortars, are pounding the neighbourhood of Trnovaca. Units -- 30-strong units from Voljevac has been sent to Makljen Vakuf, and the town is completely blocked and the settlement of Uzricje has to be cleared to allow entrance into the city. And the order has been received to prepare for an infantry attack. Infantry units are attacking from the town, and in the centre there are strongholds of the army, the BH army at Rajici has received reinforcements. They have a mortar above Duratbegovic. At 1550 fierce shelling has started of the town and the surroundings," and then it goes on to talk about the concentration of forces. I don't want to paraphrase the whole document. Tell me, what is true from the report?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see who wrote it, but I think a major part of this report is either a justification or somebody showing off. It is true that we blocked the Duratbegovic Dolac, that we tried to defend ourselves from Dolac because Colonel Siljeg ordered all-out attack on Gornji Vakuf. It is not true that on the 12th of January we fired a single shell into the area inhabited by Croats. It is not true that Trnovaca was shelled. And my parents were captured at Trnovaca on that day. If we had been ready to attack the HVO, surely I would have sent my parents away from Trnovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. How people would have acted is a moot point; some remained in their homes in spite of the military activity and tried to defend their homes. But do you know Mr. Pero Mejdandzic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the first commander of the HVO in Gornji Vakuf, the top commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How would you describe your cooperation with him and how would you assess him as a commander?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wanted to cooperate; there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you considered him to be a serious and responsible individual?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was a serious man; that's what I thought at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at the following document now 4D 00341.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question. In this document it says that a thousand soldiers had massed in Vakuf. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in Gornji Vakuf a thousand men -- well that figure just can't be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, when it was formed how many men about the 317th Mountain Brigade have?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the armed forces in Gornji Vakuf consisted of 2.560 men; they had a brigade and Municipal TO staff and a total of 2.560 member.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the 317th, is that the number for the 317th?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For the total number of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the 317th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was up to establishment strength and it had 2.137 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you added to that number the members of the armija of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Jajce who were in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that the 1st Battalion was formed and the command of the 305th, and they had their command positions and they were with their battalions in Voljica. The brigade wasn't in Vakuf at the time that you are mentioning. The brigade had a battalion and a half at the defence line facing Kupres. The other part of the unit was positioned from Voljevac up to Duratbegovic Dolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Voljevac is in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 4D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, so as not to waste time given the Defence hypothesis according to which it was the ABiH that launched the attack not the HVO - well, this is a hypothesis that the Judges will have to assess in the light of the evidence presented - but if one assumes that this hypothesis is real, if one is launching an attack in military terms, aren't those who are on leave called back? You said that the brigade had a third at the line, a third in reserve, and one-third of its men on leave. So if one assumes that the Defence hypothesis is correct, if one assumes that the ABiH was bringing reinforcements, wouldn't that mean that those men who were on leave should have been called back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, counsel didn't put that question to me, but all the commanders called back the men who were on leave, but it doesn't make sense to have a thousand men in town; it's not wise in military terms because the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So where did you keep these men if it wasn't wise to keep them in town?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look.
