And the commander had nothing in common with the image we have of commanders in armies such as the States, France, Britain, but he also had to be the father and the mother and political commissar to explain system. He had to be a psychologist. He also had to be brave, not to be afraid, to at least partly control those units. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I see. As no political solution was found and armies didn't have a Joint Command, they didn't know who was to the left, who was to the right, what kind of equipment they had, this also contributed to lack of confidence between units and commanders. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main problem, after all, was that they didn't want a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's quite right. Do you know that Mr. Franjo Tudjman in 1992 literally appealed to Mr. Izetbegovic when the agreement was signed in Split: Let's make a military agreement for the simple reason that we'll have one enemy and one theatre of war. If there is one enemy, then the theatre of war is one and the same, and those who are fighting that enemy must be linked together under a single command with the same logistics and so on. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know why this was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said do you know why this was not implemented. Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of July in the territory of Central Bosnia Mr. Tolo arrived. I can't remember now his first name, but I remember the man and what he said. He had an order from General Bobetko which said that joint units be formed or commands and that units in the brigades should be mixed; and that in areas with a majority Bosniak population the commander should be a Bosniak; and in areas where the majority population are Croats, the commander should be a Croat. This was partially implemented in Bugojno, and that command survived for about a month in Bugojno, but nowhere else in Central Bosnia was this achieved, because in my town the HVO did not want that. I say that with full responsibility. And Mr. Tolo, after a meeting in Bugojno, was brought to Rodic by the HVO, and he was allegedly released to go to Gornji Vakuf. And he reached the Serb army in Kupres, and I think he was detained there until the end of the war. And that is those discussion -- that is when discussions along those lines were discontinued. And the army even gave him the best vehicle we had because of his good -- because of our good intentions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was released a little earlier, but that's not so important. You have testified about my efforts over two months to have a Joint Command. Let me ask you now: Are you aware that what we have been discussing at length, and that is the order on the resubordination of units, that this order was signed by Bozo Rajic, a minister in the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I know that there were commissions, and you were a member of one such commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And at the meeting in Gornji Vakuf on the 4th of November, you signed that agreement, among others, and I was informed about it. One of your obligations in forming joint units was to return weapons to the army in Prozor. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But none of that was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's not did into that. I'm talking about joint commands. Joint Command you can achieve only if the army commanders agree. We can make endeavours and, if you can remember, I think we achieved some good results, at least in my opinion. In Ramo, people were returned. For two months there was absolutely nothing more than perhaps village quarrels. I think Central Bosnia was stabilised to a certain extent. I don't know whether you're aware that I had joint actions with Mr. Merdan at Komar. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of my role in the defence of Travnik after the fall of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening I was at Plava Voda, you may have forgotten, when General Prkacin and Jasmin Jaganjac, and General Merdan, and Arif Pasalic were there. I was there that evening, and I remember that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Somewhere up there nothing was achieved. We did achieve up to a point, but I could not reach Sefer Halilovic and this was a question of politics, not us. A political solution should have been imposed on the military. Do you know that I in Zagreb just before that had lengthy talks with Mr. Izetbegovic, begging him to allow the so-called resubordination - and I will ask you what that means in military terms - because unless that is done and a political solution is delayed, inevitably military conflicts would break out and no one will be able to prevent them. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's us move on to the next document dated the 26th of October after the -- after the conflict. 3D 00484. It is a report of General Prkacin. And when I say "General Prkacin," he is not an HVO general. He's not an HV general. He's a general of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you aware that Ante Prkacin, a Croat, was a general in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here's the document -- no 3D 00484.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have it --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the ELMO now. It's a lengthy document. Just look through it, and I will ask you whether you're aware of the following -- may I speak while you're reading?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Jajce, in the month of October 1992, what was the structure of the HVO and the BH army in Travnik, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigades started to be formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So that was the embryo of the army in other words, and there was a very realistic danger for the Serbs after the fall of Jajce simply to march through and reach Sarajevo. In -- in a military sense, was that a realistic danger?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when that stampedo started from Jajce. I can give my own comment, but I don't think they would have reached Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, you're professional soldier, but the word "I don't believe" does not exist in the army. There's a real estimate of the forces up there. They were poor, disorganised, and they were in embryo form. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The structure of the -- of the army was not bad. In Busovaca it was poor; in Vitez, too; but I think Travnik was well-organised, in my judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have time, but I would be glad to discuss it with you. And then Ante Prkacin, general of the ABiH, a Croat, gathered a great force and in Capljina we equipped them, armed them completely, and sent them to assist Jajce to Turbet, to Vlasic, to the front lines. And this was done in order to prevent the very possible breakthrough of the Serbs. And what happened? They were stopped immediately after Gornji Vakuf; that's what it says here. They were maltreated for three days and returned without having been let through.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was in Bugojno, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying after Vakuf. That's what I said. It was on those routes up there. They were sent back. Not only were they sent back, a group of military policemen was also sent back. Do you know that I managed to get through because I'm a big man and I make a lot of noise; I'm theatrical. Do you know that I managed to get through a group of men? And naturally, I took over the command of the HVO in Travnik, and my cooperation with ABiH in Plava Voda was excellent. We quickly dug trenches around Travnik. Are you aware of any of this?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you were in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you understand how this worked, the Croats with the HVO? People had armed themselves somehow, but they didn't receive any salaries. They would buy equipment for themselves. Some men had boots, others didn't, they had their own clothes; but those people weren't parts of military structures or the armies that we're referring to, do you know how they reacted to the fact that 400 men had been sent back? 400 men who were sent to assist were sent back because the ABiH wouldn't let them through in October, and 80 per cent of those who got through were Muslims. Can you imagine the feeling that provoked? And this was just the result of a lack of trust.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that question addressed to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How did the Bosniaks -- well, how do you how think the Bosniaks in Prozor felt after that and the Bosniaks in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Not well.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had matters in Prozor, that would have been prevented. A lot of Prozor -- a lot of people in Prozor went missing and we don't know where they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Prozor, in Bugojno, throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina that is the case. There are a lot of people who went missing. But now I'm talking about what you were talking about, about the causal relationship, how oil was added to the fire. Everything had a cumulative effect, and much force was needed to keep things under control for several months while waiting for a political solution at whatever level. Is what I'm saying correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the following document -- I don't know what the number is right now. Could we place it on the ELMO, please. P 00413. I found the number. P 00413. On the ELMO. The 28th of August, 1992, is the date. This is two months before the conflict in Prozor. Zejnil Delalic issues the following order on the basis of a problem or an incident he says that occurred on the 27th of August, and this is ordered to some of the problem. He says: "Withdraw all the forces from Prozor from the joint positions and establish a defence, line us immediately in front of the town in the direction from which you were expecting the enemy to make a breakthrough. And evacuate the Muslim population from Barde, Bacevo Polje, and from other hamlets, and find accommodation in the town of Prozor. Fortify access routes by using traditional means unless armoured units try to make a breakthrough, and link up the disconnected defence lines." Zejnil Delalic was an important commander in Konjic and the surroundings at the time, and in Prozor. Is what is stated here correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Zejnil Delalic was the commander of the Tactical Group 1 on Igman, and I know that Prozor wasn't part of his zone of responsibility. I don't know how it is that he had the right to issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I don't know either, but these orders are terrible. This was two months before the conflict in Rama, two months before he was preparing for possible problems. My question is: Both sides on every day was looking in -- at what the other side was doing in its own backyard and wondering what they would do. This is a tradition military fear. One is afraid of someone who isn't under Joint Command, and everything is still open, all possibilities are still open. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, both of you. Frankly, when I read this order I do not see that this order was in a way kind of inciting further incidents, because, for example, in paragraph 4 the order says, and I quote: "Try to make the Prozor War Presidency and the HVO municipal headquarters in Prozor coordinate their separate lines of defence." Although it is true that the order speaks about separate lines of defence, but anyway, it also speaks about coordination, which in my view is a positive sign. And also, the very last sentence says, and I quote: "Write up a detailed report on the causes and perpetrators of the incident on either side." So for me it is -- it is not a kind of belligerent approach, but it -- probably the intention was to go along and -- with the -- and to be a kind of cooperation between the two sides, but it is my interpretation it. I wonder if General Praljak or Brigadier Agic could confirm that. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, in wartime nothing is so sensitive and so terrible as abandoning positions at joint lines of defence. This amounts to betrayal, and it's quite inconceivable within the army. This provokes a maximum lack of trust, because men's lives are at stake. You are at line and there is an order and it says withdraw from the line because there is a problem. Everything else is quite simple according to my interpretation. Perhaps the brigadier could also tell us whether this is an extremely difficult and incomprehensible form, not of violating military discipline, but this is an extremely incomprehensible way of acting. People can be executed in the army because of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a document here signed by Delalic, but apparently it's said that he didn't have the authority to send orders to Prozor but let's leave that aside for the moment. Well, this document states, as General Praljak has pointed out, it states in paragraph 1 that the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina requested - and these forces were under the command of the municipality of Prozor - these forces requested to withdraw from the joint positions, the positions facing the Serbs. As a soldier, what is your opinion of that? What did this in fact signify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the person who signed this didn't have the right to sign such an order; that's the first thing. I don't know whether General Praljak will believe me, but this is the first time I've heard of an incident in Prozor on the 27th of August, an incident that provoked this. Sabic never informed us of anything of the kind. In Prozor things were functioning as well as possible at the time, because I know there were two soldiers manning howitzers; I'm aware of that fact and this order surprised me. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was this person a spy, an agent?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's read through the following: "Consultations with the Supreme Command of the armed forces in Sarajevo ordered." So those consultations with the supreme command of the armed forces being urgently ordered.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary for me to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Naturally, but here's another question to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another issue that is very important. This order issued by the Supreme Command of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo states that villages should be evacuated and three villages are mentioned. They state that the -- it states that the Muslim population should be evacuated from these three villages, because there was allegedly an incident on the 27th of August. As far as you know, at the time was there any movement of Muslim -- of the Muslim population as a result of an order issued by the Territorial Defence? That's what this document seems to indicate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's not the supreme command that issued this, it's the commander of the Tactical Group, Zejnil Delalic, who issued this order and I really don't know about this. I'm not aware of this incident in Prozor either. This wasn't in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps; this was outside their zone of responsibility, the zone of responsibility of the District Staff in Zenica. I believe that this did happen, but I'm really not familiar with this event. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That answer is quite correct. I'm just trying to find an explanation for the way in which the war is provoked by referring to documents, the fear people felt, alcohol abuse, et cetera, et cetera. I'm just trying to clarify certain issues with you, and I'm interested in clarifying this for both sides. Let's understand each other. I'm just talking about pouring oil onto the fire, those sort of things. But I have another question I would now like to put to you, and I will show you a document that relates to this question. Could we have the following document on the ELMO, please -- how many ABiH officers came from the JNA in the late autumn and summer of 1992, after they had spent the entire war against Croatia in the JNA, do you know the figure?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't known the figure. I know the figure for the armed forces in Gornji Vakuf. We had a total of five officers who were former JNA members; four officers were concerned and one non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I have a document we could place on the ELMO here. Here's my question: Mr. Selmo Cikotic was a Montenegrin Muslim before the war and he was in the air force?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the PVO, anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic arrived in April. Mr. Mendevac [phoen], Merdan, Hadzihasanovic, all the men we have mentioned here. Mr. Halilovic is from Sandzak, from Serbia. At the time of the attack of the JNA, they were all members of the JNA under the command of General Kadijevic and others. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not familiar with all the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And they were also under the command of Mr. Stipe Mesic for a certain period of time. Can we place this document on the ELMO? In this document that you will have a look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a number? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I received it today, Your Honours. We'll -- it will be given a number. Could you please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The date is the 5th of August, 1994. Decision on promoting within the Army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and was signed by Alija Izetbegovic. There are 227 names, and not a single name can be found that is not a Muslim, Bosniak, name. Is there a single name that isn't the name of a Muslim or a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on page 1, under C, the first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abu Mali.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- that Abu Mali was one of the al-Qaeda terrorists who is on the list of terrorists established by the Security Council of the UN?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Read through another two names. What did he command? It says which unit he commanded. Could you read it through.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The El Mujahid detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There are two others. Someone for morale and religious affairs, and there's another individual from El Mujahid. So we have three from the El Mujahid brigade, and they were made regular officers of the ABiH. Is what I have said correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it's correct. This has been signed by the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since we're addressing this issue let's clarify the matter -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Or perhaps we don't have any more time, Your Honours, unfortunately. It seems it's late. We can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll clarify this tomorrow. It's now 7.00 p.m., and it's time to adjourn. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I invite everyone to return tomorrow. The witness shouldn't take any documents away with him, so as to avoid being influenced; and if everything goes well, the cross-examination should be completed tomorrow. Thank you. And I will see you all tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
